title: Small Bets, Big Impact Building GenBI at a Fortune 100 – Asaf Bord, Northwestern Mutual

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on a modular four-agent architecture—metadata, RAG, SQL, and BI agents—each independently productizable with orchestration and governance layers. GenBI is an analytics copilot for enterprise BI workflows at a Fortune 100 financial services company, spanning data analytics and enterprise operations. The system has delivered production impact with the RAG agent automating report routing, while A/B testing and Databricks Genie evaluation represent ongoing assessment. The content assumes familiarity with BI workflows, RAG, and multi-agent design but is framed as an accessible case study rather than deep technical internals. The talk presents a real-world deployment narrative at Northwestern Mutual with measured outcomes and lessons learned. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with supporting excerpts and character anchors.

summary: Asaf Bord introduces GenBI as an LLM-powered agent that helps users answer business questions with data, aiming for data democratization without reliance on BI teams. Northwestern Mutual's 160-year history and generational responsibility create a highly risk-averse culture making large uncertain AI investments difficult. Bord identifies four core challenges: lack of precedent, using real messy data rather than synthetic data, overcoming blind-trust bias around accuracy, and justifying budget to leadership. The team chose real data to surface production complexities early and embedded business users as advocates in the research process. Trust-building involved a sandbox environment, no real client data, and a crawl-walk-run release strategy: first to BI experts, then business managers, and eventually executives only when accuracy is sufficient. The system initially avoids generating SQL, routing users to existing certified reports instead. The incremental roadmap gives leadership visibility and plug-pulling ability at any phase. Phase one researched natural language to SQL. Phase two defined good metadata for a BI agent, benefiting a separate semantic-layer initiative. Phase three delivered multi-context semantic search packaged as a data-finder product. The architecture includes four agents—metadata, RAG, SQL, and BI—plus governance, trust, orchestration, and contextual UI layers. Each agent can be packaged as its own product with tangible business impact. The RAG agent automated roughly 80% of the 20% of BI team capacity spent routing reports, freeing about two full-time equivalents on a 10-person team. Metadata learnings enabled A/B tests proving LLM performance gains from enriched metadata, justifying continued investment. The incremental approach eliminates sunk-cost bias, creates benchmarks for evaluating third-party solutions like Databricks Genie, and ensures value delivery quarter over quarter. Bord closes with future thoughts on data preparation tools, task-specific models, copilot user proximity, model security, and GenAI-era SaaS pricing shifts from seats to usage or value-based models.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Bord introduces himself and GenBI as a fusion of GenAI and BI. He explains Northwestern Mutual's profile, why it is a strong place for GenAI (data, money, use cases, talent), and why it is hard (risk aversion rooted in decades-long client commitments).

sections.title: Four Core Challenges
sections.summary: Bord outlines four challenges: no precedent for GenBI, using real messy data, building trust with users and leadership around accuracy, and securing budget in a risk-averse culture.

sections.title: Using Real Data and Real Users
sections.summary: The team chose real messy data to understand production complexities early. Working with actual data users provided subject matter expertise, real eval examples, and created business buy-in, with end users pulling the product forward.

sections.title: Building Trust with Management
sections.summary: Bord describes sandbox usage, no client data, and a crawl-walk-run release strategy starting with BI experts, then business managers, and eventually executives only when accuracy is sufficient. The system initially avoids SQL generation, routing to certified reports instead.

sections.title: Incremental Roadmap and Phases
sections.summary: Bord details the incremental approach giving leadership visibility and plug-pulling ability. Phase one was research on NL-to-SQL. Phase two defined good metadata for a BI agent, benefiting a separate semantic-layer initiative. Phase three delivered semantic search packaged as a standalone data-finder product.

sections.title: Why the Incremental Approach Worked
sections.summary: Bord explains that six-week sprints produced tangible deliverables, transparent progress, and incremental business value. The approach eliminates sunk-cost bias and creates benchmarks for evaluating third-party solutions like Databricks Genie, enabling informed build-vs-buy decisions.

sections.title: Architecture and Agent Pipeline
sections.summary: Bord details the four-agent architecture: metadata agent for context, RAG agent for finding certified reports, SQL agent for queries when reports are insufficient, and BI agent for translating results into business answers. Each agent is independently productizable with governance, trust, orchestration, and contextual UI layers.

sections.title: Business Impact and Next Steps
sections.summary: The RAG agent automated about 80% of the 20% of BI capacity spent routing reports, freeing roughly two full-time equivalents. Metadata learnings enabled A/B tests proving enriched metadata improves LLM performance. Next steps include evaluating Databricks Genie and enriching the catalog with metadata.

sections.title: Future Thoughts and SaaS Pricing
sections.summary: Bord shares thoughts on data preparation tools, task-specific models, copilot user proximity, and model security. He highlights a shift in SaaS pricing from seats to usage or value-based models, citing Salesforce Data Cloud as an early example, and argues this will reshape SaaS economics regardless of whether products are GenAI.
